articles.title: Your Customer Ordered Black, Large. Your Supplier Shipped Blue, Medium.
articles.excerpt: The wrong parcel is rarely the supplier's first mistake A customer orders a black hoodie in size Large. Two weeks later she opens a blue one in Medium. She emails you a photo of the shipping label nex…
articles.body: The wrong parcel is rarely the supplier's first mistake A customer orders a black hoodie in size Large. Two weeks later she opens a blue one in Medium. She emails you a photo of the shipping label next to the item — exactly the evidence AliExpress asks for in a wrong-item claim — and she is right to be annoyed. The instinct is to blame the supplier. In most cases I audit, the supplier shipped exactly what the order told them to ship. The error happened earlier, in the mapping between your store variant and the supplier variant. Variant mapping is the link that says: when someone picks "Black / Large" on your product page, place an AliExpress order for that supplier's specific SKU for black, large.
articles.author: jinguo ren

articles.title: Why Date.now() can return values that go backwards
articles.excerpt: Here's a JavaScript snippet that, on rare occasions in production, will fail: const start = Date.now(); doSomeWork(); const end = Date.now(); const elapsed = end - start; console.log(`Took ${elapsed}m…
articles.body: Here's a JavaScript snippet that, on rare occasions in production, will fail: const start = Date . now ( ) ; doSomeWork ( ) ; const end = Date . now ( ) ; const elapsed = end - start ; console . log ( `Took ${elapsed}ms` ) ; // → Sometimes: "Took -1832ms" How can end be smaller than start ? The work happened in real time, and the calls were sequential. What's going on? Date.now() reads the wall clock Date.now() returns the system wall clock, the same clock shown in your operating system's status bar. That clock can be changed underneath your program: Clock step corrections. Time-sync daemons normally slew the clock (speed it up or slow it down a little), which never goes backwards. But when the offset is large, they step it.

articles.excerpt: The page says the checkout health check failed. The responder sees a red status tile, a recent deployment, and a new pricing rule behind a flag. Treat this as a hypothetical incident: the immediate pr…
articles.body: The page says the checkout health check failed. The responder sees a red status tile, a recent deployment, and a new pricing rule behind a flag. Treat this as a hypothetical incident: the immediate problem is deciding whether to disable the rule, while the evidence currently proves only that a check failed. A dashboard full of red does not establish which customers were exposed or whether the rule caused their failures. Short answer: for HTTP health checks with polling in Node.js, choose a small request interface that lets you set a timeout, inspect the response, and retain the result of every attempt. Add a poller that records timing and prevents overlapping attempts.

articles.title: Building a Client-Side Audio Silence Remover with Web Audio API (Zero Server Uploads)
articles.excerpt: Markdown title: "Building a Client-Side Audio Silence Remover with Web Audio API (Zero Server Uploads)" Handling media files online usually involves sending multi-megabyte payloads to a cloud worker,…
articles.body: Markdown title: "Building a Client-Side Audio Silence Remover with Web Audio API (Zero Server Uploads)" published: true tags: webdev, javascript, audio, productivity cover_image: Handling media files online usually involves sending multi-megabyte payloads to a cloud worker, waiting in a server queue, and downloading the output. For audio processing tasks like removing awkward pauses from podcasts or interviews, this architecture is inefficient and introduces unnecessary data privacy risks. With modern browser capabilities, heavy server-side processing is no longer mandatory for these tasks. In this post, we’ll explore how to detect and trim dead air directly inside the client using the native Web Audio API —the same local-first philosophy powering the audio suite at BuzzyTools .

articles.title: Could Cleo's AI App Really Get You $250? The FTC Says Rarely
articles.excerpt: Cleo calls itself an "AI money coach," and the FTC says its ads promised cash advances of up to $250. In its 2025 complaint, the FTC alleged that the app almost never showed your amount until after yo…
articles.body: Cleo calls itself an "AI money coach," and the FTC says its ads promised cash advances of up to $250. In its 2025 complaint, the FTC alleged that the app almost never showed your amount until after you paid for a subscription, that most Plus users with an advance got under $45, that "today" cash cost an extra $3.99 to $9.99 fee, and that some people couldn't cancel while they owed an advance. Cleo settled for $17 million without admitting or denying the allegations, and its general counsel called the claims inaccurate. Starting October 27, 2026, the FTC is sending about 2.1 million PayPal payments, more than $15.8 million in total, to people who paid for eligible instant advances. The FTC hasn't said how much each person gets.

articles.title: NASA wants you to 'shine bright' today for Voyager 1's light-day milestone. Here's how
articles.excerpt: NASA invites the public to shine lights in Morse code after sunset today (Nov. 17) to celebrate Voyager 1 reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth.
articles.body: As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft. The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth . And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.
